title: Corners, islands and internal storage
intro: Special cabinets need more than nominal volume. Review corner access, island movement and internal hardware against contents and actual product information.

sections.title: Distinguish corner volume from access
sections.text: Draw the corner opening and contents, then compare fixed shelving and pull-out systems for opening size, operating sweep, cleaning and removal. Volume alone does not prove access. A product image does not establish handing or carcass compatibility.
sections.caption: Access includes operation, cleaning and replacement.

sections.title: Test the island in context
sections.text: Test the island with open drawers, occupied seating and passing routes, including simultaneous opposing openings. An appliance or sink introduces a separate service-coordination item. Its appearance on a plan does not prove feasible or approved service connections.
sections.caption: Test the island during opening and work.

sections.title: Select hardware using its data
sections.text: Record manufacturer, model, handing, opening requirements, sweep and rated loading with conditions. Compare actual contents and tool access. A hinge, handle or front change reopens the assembly review; individually suitable parts may still conflict when combined.
sections.caption: Review the product within the complete assembly.

example.title: Worked case and decision
example.text: The mechanism fits the carcass but a handle prevents the front opening far enough. Review front, handle and hinge together against product data, then retest the sweep without improvising changes to the mechanism.
example.decision: Decision: establish assembly compatibility before approval.

quiz.question: Does fitting inside the carcass establish operability?
quiz.explanation: Operation depends on the front, neighbors and service access.

assignment.prompt: Submit corner/island layouts, opening states, a hardware card and a conflict decision.

faq.question: Is the largest volume always better storage?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Contents, reach, cleaning and movement determine usable value.
